title: IBM and Rutgers Control Quantum Chaos Across 100 Qubits on Heron Processor - Quantum Computing Report
gist: Rutgers, IBM Quantum and collaborators demonstrated real-time feedback control across 100 qubits of the 156-qubit IBM Heron processor ibm_fez, using nearly 5,000 two-qubit gates and nearly 5,000 mid-circuit resets, and characterized a control-induced phase transition near pc = 0.495(1). Published in Nature Physics, it is described as one of the largest realizations of real-time feedback and non-unitary adaptive circuits to date.

insights.claim: Researchers from Rutgers University, IBM Quantum and partner institutions demonstrated real-time quantum feedback control across 100 qubits on the 156-qubit IBM Quantum Heron processor ibm_fez, published in Nature Physics.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Peer-reviewed validation of IBM hardware running mid-circuit measurement and reset at scale.
insights.locator: Researchers from Rutgers University, IBM Quantum

insights.claim: The experiment executed nearly 5,000 two-qubit entangling gates and nearly 5,000 mid-circuit measurement-based resets across 100 linearly connected qubits.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Gate and reset counts are a concrete benchmark of dynamic-circuit capability.

insights.claim: The study is one of the largest experimental realizations of real-time feedback and non-unitary adaptive circuits to date, validating matrix product state models and statistical mechanics mappings on physical hardware.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Theory-hardware agreement supports the credibility of dynamic-circuit approaches.
insights.quote: one of the largest experimental realizations of real-time feedback and non-unitary adaptive circuits to date
insights.locator: The study marks one of the largest

insights.claim: By competing information-scrambling operations against local resets that push qubits toward zero, the team observed a dynamical control-induced phase transition (CIPT) between a chaotic volume-law phase and a controlled unentangled phase.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Shows measurable physics emerging from the balance of scrambling and feedback on real hardware.

insights.claim: The critical point sits at pc = 0.495(1) with exponents nu = 1.05(2), z = 2.08(1) and beta = 1.05(2); the chaotic volume-law phase spans 0 <= p < 0.3 and the controlled phase 0.5 < p <= 1.0.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Precise critical exponents give a quantitative reference for later hardware comparisons.

insights.claim: The adaptive circuits provide experimental validation of non-unitary dynamics that the article calls critical for scalable quantum error correction.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Feedback and reset capability is a prerequisite for fault-tolerant roadmaps.
insights.locator: Researchers from Rutgers University, IBM Quantum

insights.claim: Across 10,000 shots per circuit configuration, Kullback-Leibler divergence comparisons against classical dephasing Markov models indicated the processor sampled a genuine quantum random process rather than incoherent noise.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Statistical certification method helps separate real quantum signal from classical noise in noisy devices.
insights.locator: To distinguish true coherent quantum dynamics
